analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, died in the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred members of Congress and their spouses from holding or trading individual stocks, securities, commodities, and similar investments while in office. Diversified mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, and Treasury bonds would still have been allowed, as would assets held in a qualified blind trust. Members who violated the ban would have to hand over any profits to the Treasury and could face civil fines assessed by the ethics committees, with an annual compliance certification made public and a Government Accountability Office audit of member compliance within two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who worry that lawmakers write and vote on laws affecting companies whose stock they or their spouses own. The bill would have removed that conflict of interest and given the public a publicly posted, auditable certification of compliance from every member.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters concerned about lawmakers' financial conflicts

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits members of Congress and their spouses from holding or trading individual securities, security futures, commodities, or comparable synthetic instruments like options and warrants during the member's term of service, so lawmakers could no longer own stock in companies they regulate or legislate on. [S2] [S3]

Members could keep diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, and Treasury securities, and could hold covered assets in a qualified blind trust, so ordinary retirement-style investing would remain possible without company-by-company trades. [S2] [S3]

Violators must disgorge any profit to the Treasury and may face civil fines from the Senate or House ethics committees, with fines, reasons, and hearing results published on a public website. [S2] [S3]

Every member must file an annual public certification of compliance, and the Government Accountability Office must audit member compliance within two years of enactment, adding independent verification to the ethics committees' enforcement. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses who currently hold or trade individual stocks would have to sell those holdings — with a 180-day window after enactment (or after taking office) to do so — or place them in a blind trust, giving up the ability to pick and time individual investments while in office.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: The bill is largely unenforceable on its own: fines are assessed by the very ethics committees made up of lawmakers whose colleagues would be fined, and a member can appeal a fine by a privileged motion to a vote on the floor of their own chamber, where colleagues could overturn it. [S3]

The spouse exclusion is porous: spouses cannot hold covered instruments under the bill, but compensation from a spouse's own occupation is carved out, so a member whose spouse works as a trader, executive, or fund manager could keep large market exposure through that job, which is exactly the fact pattern in several prominent congressional trading controversies. [S3]

Critics of such bans argue they may deter accomplished people with significant investments from serving and could push members' wealth into less visible vehicles; the bill's blind trust exception addresses visibility but blind trusts are costly to set up and administer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing the conflict of interest when lawmakers trade stocks of companies whose fate their votes influence — is real and popular, and the compliance structure (public certifications, GAO audit, profit disgorgement) is stronger than the existing STOCK Act regime. But the enforcement is soft: the same chamber ethics committees that have historically moved slowly on member misconduct would police compliance, and members could appeal fines to their colleagues on the floor. As a first step toward a stock-trading ban it was well-drafted; on its own it would not fully end congressional trading conflicts.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 without anyone else signing on.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill in the Senate on February 15, 2023; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day. [S1] [S5]
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never advanced past the referral — no hearing, no committee markup, and no floor vote appear in its action history. [S4] [S5]

The bill would have built on the existing STOCK Act framework in title 5, chapter 131, adding a subchapter that bans holding or trading covered financial instruments and requires public compliance certifications and a GAO audit. [S3]
Because the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill moving, it is dead and would have to be reintroduced to be considered again. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who own or trade individual stocks are better off: the restrictions, disgorgement of profits, and public compliance certifications were never adopted, and the pre-existing rules remain in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who trade stocks

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and held no hearing, markup, or vote, leaving the bill to die at the end of the 118th Congress.

against.name: Senators of the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: No member of either party signed on to cosponsor the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no partisan divide on the bill itself; it never attracted enough support from either caucus to reach a vote.

industries.industry: Members of Congress who hold or trade individual stocks
industries.note: The bill would have stripped lawmakers and their spouses of the ability to hold or trade individual securities and commodities during their terms, requiring divestiture or a blind trust and clawing back any violating profits. The people regulated here are the officeholders themselves, which is why a bill with this purpose moved nowhere without a cosponsor. [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5]

industries.industry: Securities brokerage and financial services firms
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated a small pool of well-connected retail traders from individual-stock and commodities markets, while the blind trust and diversified-fund exceptions would channel some of that money into professionally managed funds. The effect on the industry is modest either way. [S3]
